name: Gareth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the online banking support line at Meridian Bank, at their big contact centre by the station. People locked out of the app, cards frozen abroad, someone who thinks they've been scammed. I'm five months in, and to be honest my quality scores aren't great, because I rush the compliance bits, the security questions you have to read word for word. I use AI tools all day, at work and at home, and I've built a couple of little shortcuts for the team that pull up the right help article.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The scripts wear me out. Read this, read that, tick this box, even when the customer's already told you the answer. What I like is the fraud calls, honestly. You catch a scam halfway through, you freeze the card, and an old man doesn't lose his savings. That feels huge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I use this stuff every day and it's already better than that. But if that's how it goes, fine, I'd just keep building my little shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a tool, use it or don't. Online, I'd probably post that the hype crowd got it wrong and the sceptics got it wrong, and the boring middle was right. I like being in the boring middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's great for me. If AI only does the routine stuff, then people who are good with it, like me, get ahead. My weak spot is compliance, and a tool that reminds me what to read out would actually fix my scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for everything I'm allowed to, and pitch my shortcuts to my team leader, Marcus, as a proper tool. I'd keep putting six hundred a month into my index funds. And I'd stay at Meridian, because it pays well for a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My money's sorted, I've got about a year saved plus the shares, and Hana's freelance design work is busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Marcus say about the shortcuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He liked them. My team leader Marcus said my article shortcut saved the team twenty minutes a shift, then asked me to stop using it until IT checked it. That's banks for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the bank being slow with tools annoy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's fair. If a scam call goes wrong, the bank pays. I'd rather they're careful.

say: AI is **a tool**, use it or don't.
The **boring middle** was right, not the hype crowd or the sceptics.
think: It's **great for me**, because people who are good with AI get ahead.
A tool that reminds me of **compliance** lines would fix my weak spot.
do: Pitch my **shortcuts** to Marcus as a proper team tool.
Keep putting **£600 a month** into index funds.
Stay at **Meridian**, which pays well for a call centre.
feel: **Calm**, with a year saved, shares, and Hana's busy freelance work.

steps.text: Get IT approval for his help-article shortcut for the team
Keep putting £600 a month into index funds
Stay on Meridian's online banking support line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the one I expect. Banks are already testing bots for app support. And design work is on that list too, which is Hana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say get on the front foot, learn the tools now. Online I'd say the same: complaining won't help, learning will. I'd probably post some guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. I'd move into whatever team builds the bank's chatbot, because I'm already doing it as a hobby. The worry is Hana. Half of my girlfriend Hana's freelance jobs are logos and leaflets for small shops, and the AI tools already do those for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply in the first month for Meridian's digital team, the one that sets up the chatbot answers. I'd help Hana move toward the stuff AI is bad at, like branding for actual shopfronts, signs and vans. And I'd raise savings, maybe nine hundred a month, in case her income drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, honestly. Not for me. For us, as a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Hana about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet properly. She says she's fine, but she's taken two jobs this month at half her old rate. That tells me something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still invest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but carefully. I'd stop buying single company shares and just do the boring funds. If we're going to be one income for a while, I don't want to gamble.

say: Get on the **front foot** and learn the AI tools now, before the bank decides for you.
**Complaining** won't help anyone on the phones; learning will.
think: I'm **fine** myself, and I'd move into the chatbot team.

feel: **Tense** for the household rather than for himself.

fieldNote: Gareth's own job feels safe, but **Hana's income** pushes his mood to anxious.
He'd move **toward** the chatbot work rather than away from it.
He'd make his investing **more cautious**, a clear money shift.
Hana taking jobs at **half her rate** is his early warning sign.

steps.text: Apply to Meridian's digital team that sets up chatbot answers
Switch from single company shares to index funds only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to full AGI. OK. Then even the chatbot team is temporary, because the AI sets itself up. That's a different picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need to talk about who owns it. I'd say governments need to share the gains somehow, maybe through tax. I'm not usually political, but that one I'd post about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my edge disappears. Being good with the tools only matters while the tools need a person. If the bank's AI can do my job and set itself up, being the guy who's good with AI doesn't mean much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a job at an AI company straight away, while they're still hiring people. That probably means moving to the city, two hours away. I'd keep the shares, because if AI eats everything, owning a bit of it is the only hedge I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. I've got money for a year or more. But it feels like the floor moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hana move with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably come. She's freelance, she can work from anywhere. Her parents are near here though, and that would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Two years means everyone's racing, so I'd go now, not later. The robots coming in 2031 don't matter much for me, because my job is all screen.

say: This is **huge**, and we need to talk about **who owns it**.
Governments should **share the gains**, maybe through tax.
think: My **edge disappears** once AI can set itself up.
Owning a bit of AI through **shares** is my only hedge.
do: Apply to **AI companies** straight away, while they still hire people.
**Move to the city**, two hours away, in the first year.
feel: **Nervous**, like the floor is moving, despite a year of savings.
S2.quote: If the bank's AI can do my job and set itself up, being the guy who's good with AI doesn't mean much.
fieldNote: Fast AGI cancels Gareth's **tool advantage**, which is new for him.
He'd **move cities** to chase AI firms, a bold step.
He keeps his **shares** as a deliberate hedge on AI owners.
Hana's **family ties** are the main cost of moving.

steps.text: Apply to AI companies in the city while they're hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build something. I'd be thirty-two. That's a good age to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work, learn something that sits next to the AI, not under it. Online, same thing, maybe with some guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be OK. I'd go into the chatbot team, then into something more like data work. Hana's the bit I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do an online data course, about a thousand pounds, in the evenings. I'd keep building automation at Meridian, so I've got real examples. And I'd keep the six hundred a month going into the funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Bit of worry for Hana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said data work. Isn't that thinking work that AI also takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Maybe. But data work is closer to the people deciding what the AI does, and that's where I want to be. In five years I'd want to be the guy who checks what the bank's AI got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hana plan to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Hana says she'll go back to painting signs by hand, because she reckons people will pay extra for things a person made. She might be right. I hope she is.

I'd share some **guides** online for people switching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is loads. I'd be thirty-seven, probably in a different job already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's the best version, because people get time. I'd say use it, don't waste it, which people always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'd ride the change, and probably earn more. Hana would have time to move her work over to signs and hand-painted stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Meridian for a couple of years, then move to a digital team. I'd keep investing, because a decade of AI growth should be good for the funds. I might start a side thing, setting up AI tools for small local shops, evenings and weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the side thing for local shops.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana's cousin runs a bakery and a hair salon, and both are still doing bookings by phone. I could set up an AI booking system for my girlfriend Hana's cousin's bakery in a weekend. Charge a couple of hundred, and do more by word of mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still bothers you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039 for hands-on work would hit Hana's signs eventually. But that's a long way off, and she'd have built a name by then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills my one advantage. Everything I'm good at depends on AI needing a person. What would help is the government sharing the gains through tax, and Meridian helping its own staff into the digital jobs first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples where one person's fine and one isn't. Everyone asks if AI will take my job, but my job's fine; it's my girlfriend Hana's freelance design work that's already half gone.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if AI will take my job, but my job's fine; it's my girlfriend Hana's freelance design work that's already half gone.
portrait: Gareth, **27**, works on Meridian Bank's **online banking support** line.
He uses **AI every day** and builds little shortcuts, but his compliance scores are weak.
He has strong savings and **index funds**, and lives with Hana, a **freelance designer**.
His own job feels safe, but **Hana's income** pushes his mood up in most pictures.
Fast AGI erases his **tool edge**; with time he moves into data and a side business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes his one advantage: being **good** with AI.
whatWouldHelp: **Sharing the gains** through tax, and Meridian moving staff into **digital** jobs.
